notes: Fareham operates mandatory HMO licensing only. There is no selective licensing and no additional HMO licensing scheme. A licence is only needed for HMOs let to five or more people forming two or more households who share facilities.
research: The council page sets out the licensing position in full and describes only the national mandatory regime: 'An HMO licence is required if all of the following apply: It has five or more occupiers comprising two or more separate households, regardless of number of storeys...' and 'From 1 October 2018, mandatory licensing is no longer limited to HMOs that are three or more storeys high, but includes buildings with one or two storeys.' The words 'selective licensing' and 'additional licensing' do not appear anywhere on the page. The page also covers HHSRS, HMO management regulations, the public register and the joint fire safety protocol with Gosport, so it is a complete statement of the council's private-rented licensing activity. Fareham and Gosport run a shared regulatory service and the two HMO pages are near identical in wording, both mandatory-only. CORROBORATION: the Fees and Charges 2025/26 licensing section covers Licensing Act 2003 premises and personal licences, rateable-value bands and related permits, and contains no selective or additional licensing fee line. A live discretionary scheme must carry its own fee. WEAKER THAN OTHERS IN THIS BATCH: the HMO page publishes no fee at all, so corroboration is thinner than for councils whose fee tables are explicit.

notes: Fenland operates mandatory HMO licensing only, at £750 for a new licence and £660 to renew. There is no selective or additional licensing scheme. A selective scheme for Wisbech was consulted on in 2016 but was deferred and never brought in.
research: The council states the licence trigger as the national mandatory test only: 'Anyone who owns or manages a HMO... must have a licence from us if: their property is occupied by 5 or more people; occupants form 2 or more households; occupants share basic amenities'. It adds that properties rented to fewer than 5 occupiers 'must comply with HMO regulations', so regulations but no licence. Fees: new applications £750, renewals £660. A single mandatory fee line with no discretionary-scheme fee. HISTORY, checked carefully: Cabinet 21 January 2016 report 'Selective Licensing Scheme for Wisbech' recommended only to 'Approve for consultation the draft selective licensing scheme and the conditions'. Cabinet 19 January 2017 followed the consultation and the decision (minute CAB59/16) was to DEFER implementation. The member task and finish group reported to Cabinet on 22 March 2018 that 'the task group were not in agreement that implementing a discretionary Selective Licensing scheme would be the most effective course of action at this time'. Consulted on but never designated, so not recorded. FALSE POSITIVE TRAP: Fenland has instead made Article 4 Directions for small HMOs in Wisbech, which are PLANNING control. On 24 February 2025 Full Council approved an Immediate Article 4 Direction for central Wisbech (Wisbech Riverside and Wisbech South wards) and a Non-Immediate Direction for outer Wisbech (Wisbech North, Wisbech Walsoken and Waterless, Leverington and Wisbech Rural), the immediate one confirmed August 2025 and the non-immediate February 2026. The council page is explicit that these 'remove permitted development rights, requiring property owners to obtain planning permission before converting a dwelling into a small House of Multiple Occupancy'. Named wards plus commencement dates make this look like a licensing designation but it is not.

notes: Folkestone and Hythe operates mandatory HMO licensing only, at £1,130 to apply and £960 to renew. There is no selective licensing and no additional HMO licensing scheme. Smaller shared homes do not need a council licence.
research: The council states: 'All HMOs with five or more people making up two or more families will need a licence to operate. This applies regardless of their size. This is accordance with the Licensing of Houses in Multiple Occupation (Prescribed Description) (England) Order 2018.' That is the national mandatory regime and the only trigger given. The register is described as 'The public register for mandatory licensed HMOs', with no separate additional or selective register. Fees: application £1,130, renewal £960, one mandatory line only. The council's own site search for 'selective licensing' returned about 14 results, every one either a generic legislative reference or unrelated. The two relevant ones are the Private Sector Housing Enforcement Policy 2021, which merely lists the statutory offence of 'Failing to licence a house subject to selective licensing under Part 3' as a category of offence the policy would cover if it applied, and the Overview and Scrutiny Committee annual report 2024-25 recording that a presentation 'reviewed private sector housing enforcement and considered a selective licensing scheme'. Considered is not designated: there is no designation notice, no scheme page, no fee and no area map.

notes: Forest of Dean operates mandatory HMO licensing only. There is no selective licensing and no additional HMO licensing scheme. A new licence costs £240.88 to apply plus £1,091.63 on issue, and applies only to HMOs let to five or more people.
research: The council page carries the heading 'Mandatory HMO licensing' and describes only the national regime, including the flats-above-shops extension: 'Purpose built flats will also come within the definition, where there are up to two flats in the block and one or both of the flats are occupied by five or more persons in two or more separate households.' No selective or additional scheme is mentioned anywhere in the private housing section. Fees: application (Part 1) £240.88, licence issue (Part 2) new £1,091.63, renewal issue £989.13. WORDING TRAP: the same fee table includes 'Additional fee for seven or more rooms, £41.00 per additional letting room (capped at £400.00)'. That is a per-room surcharge on a mandatory HMO licence, not an additional licensing scheme under s.56, and must not be read as one. A sitemap sweep of 700 URLs returned no page containing 'selective' or 'additional licensing' in a housing context; the only 'additional' hit was a planning permissions page.

notes: Fylde operates mandatory HMO licensing only, at £1,107 for a new licence and £850 to renew. There is no selective licensing and no additional HMO licensing scheme. Selective licensing on the Fylde coast is Blackpool's scheme, a different council.
research: The council page describes only the national mandatory regime and points to the Licensing of Houses in Multiple Occupation (Prescribed Description) (England) Order 2018 for the full list of licensable types. The clinching evidence is the fee schedule, which labels every line as mandatory: 'HMO Mandatory Licence (Housing Act 2004) Up to Five Units: £1,107.00', 'Each Additional Unit: £45.00', 'HMO Licence Renewal (Housing Act 2004) Up to Five Units: £850.00', 'Each Additional Unit: £45.00'. There is no selective or additional licensing fee, which a live discretionary scheme would have to carry. IMPORTANT FALSE POSITIVE TRAP: searches for 'Fylde selective licensing' surface an article headed 'Selective Licensing Scheme to Improve Rented Properties'. Reading it shows it is about BLACKPOOL COUNCIL, not Fylde: 'A new Selective Licensing Scheme... in the inner area of Blackpool has been approved... It covers the eight inner wards of Bloomfield, Brunswick, Claremont, Talbot, Tyldesley, Warbreck, Waterloo and Victoria... The scheme begins on 1 April 2025', directing landlords to blackpool.gov.uk/selectivelicensing. 'Fylde Coast' is a sub-regional label covering Blackpool, Fylde and Wyre, so Blackpool's scheme is routinely and wrongly attributed to Fylde. None of those wards is in Fylde Borough.

notes: Gosport operates mandatory HMO licensing only. There is no selective licensing and no additional HMO licensing scheme in the borough. A licence is required only for HMOs let to five or more people forming two or more households.
research: The council states the licence trigger as the national mandatory test only: 'An HMO licence is required if all of the following apply: It has five or more occupiers comprising two or more separate households, regardless of number of storeys...' and confirms 'From 1 October 2018, mandatory licensing is no longer limited to HMOs that are three or more storeys high'. Neither 'selective licensing' nor 'additional licensing' appears. The private rented landing page lists only three items: Private tenants, the RAPS scheme, and Renters Rights Act. TRAP CHECK: RAPS (Rented Accommodation in the Private Sector) is a voluntary landlord accreditation scheme, not a licensing designation. A full sitemap sweep of 1,153 URLs returned no URL containing 'selective' or 'additional licensing'. SECOND TRAP CHECK: the council published a consultation on 23 July 2026, 'Have your say on new policies to protect private renters in Gosport'. Reading it confirms it is NOT a licensing consultation: it seeks views on a Private Rented Sector Housing Enforcement Policy and a Renters' Rights Act Civil Penalty Policy, running to 11 September 2026. No licensing designation is proposed. Fareham and Gosport share a regulatory service and both HMO pages are mandatory-only in identical terms.

notes: Gravesham operates mandatory HMO licensing only. There is no selective licensing and no additional HMO licensing scheme. The council is separately working towards an Article 4 planning direction on HMO conversions, which is not a licence.
research: Checked with extra care. The HMO page states 'If a HMO fits A. The Standard Test, or B. The Self-contained flat test, or C. The Converted building test and it has five or more people living there, and those in occupation make up more than one household (family unit), the property must have a HMO licence', under the heading 'Mandatory licensing of Houses in Multiple Occupation'. The fee page gives a single HMO fee split in two parts: new Part A £541.81 and Part B £463.81; renewal Part A £464.98 and Part B £444.93. Relevant legislation is listed as the Housing Act 2004, the 2006 Miscellaneous Provisions Regulations and the 2018 Prescribed Description Order, mandatory only. No selective or additional fee line exists. The Private sector housing index and the Licensing index each list Houses in Multiple Occupation as the only housing licence, and a sitemap sweep returned zero URLs containing 'selective' or 'additional licensing'. DECISIVE COUNCIL STATEMENT: a council news item, 'Gravesham Borough Council seeks to extend powers over HMOs', says plainly 'The council operates the national mandatory HMO licensing scheme', reports 107 licensed HMOs at the end of March 2026, and explains that Cabinet 'agreed to continue work towards the adoption of an Article 4 Direction which would see all such conversions requiring planning permission'. FALSE POSITIVE TRAP: estate agent and aggregator pages market a 'Gravesend 2026 selective licensing health check' and postcode checkers. There is no council designation, no fee and no area behind these. The genuine 2026 development is an Article 4 planning direction, which is excluded.

notes: Guildford operates mandatory HMO licensing only, at £1,037.34. There is no selective licensing and no additional HMO licensing scheme. The council states that a shared home with three or four unrelated tenants does not need a licence from it.
research: The council gives an explicit negative for additional licensing. Under 'When a licence is not needed' it states 'If there are three or four unrelated tenants living in the property that share facilities, this is still a HMO. This property will not need a HMO licence from us.' Under an additional licensing designation those very properties would need a licence, so that sentence rules one out. Fee £1,037.34, with a £25 discount for landlord-organisation members and £50 for Guildford Letting Scheme accredited landlords. One fee line only. The Housing licences index lists only an HMO licence and a caravan site licence. COMMITTEE EVIDENCE: the Cabinet report 'Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMO) Update', 19 April 2021, has a section '18. Alternative Controls: Additional Licensing and Article 4' recording that these were 'previously considered by the 2014 Overview and Scrutiny task and finish group. In 2014, the provisions were noted as being Inappropriate to Guildford's set of circumstances at that time.' It reports that 'Currently the data suggest that unlicensable HMOs that would meet the definition of an Additionally Licensed HMO are not being significantly mismanaged', and describes an additional scheme only conditionally: 'A proportion of the Council Tax data set of 1,800 student HMOs that currently do not require a licence, would need a licence to operate, if an Additional HMO Licensing Scheme was brought into force.' A committee minute separately records that 'Guildford Borough had mandatory HMO licensing only and that HMOs of 3-4 persons did not require a licence to operate lawfully.' Considered, never designated.

schemes.areaDescription: PROPOSED ONLY, not yet designated. Consultation runs from 3 August 2026 to 18 October 2026 on a Part 3 selective licensing scheme covering Central and West Bank, Appleton, Mersey and Weston and Bridgewater wards, plus LSOA E01012379 in Highfield ward. An estimated 3,485 private rented households, around 43.4 per cent of the borough's private rented stock. The licence fee is itself part of the consultation and has not been set.

notes: Halton has no licensing scheme in force today, so only mandatory HMO licensing applies. A selective licensing scheme is out to public consultation until 18 October 2026 covering four wards and part of Highfield. If you let in those areas, watch for a decision after that date.
research: Direct council statement, given twice on the private housing page: 'Local authorities have the discretionary power to introduce additional or selective licensing in relation to private rental properties or smaller Houses in Multiple Occupation. To date Halton Council has not introduced additional or selective licensing in any areas of the borough.' The same page describes only 'Mandatory HMO Licensing - A House in Multiple Occupation with 5 or more tenants must by law be licensed by the local authority.' LIVE PROPOSAL, not a designation: a separate page is headed 'Consultation on a Selective Licensing Scheme for Privately Rented Homes' and states 'Halton Borough Council is proposing to introduce a Selective Licensing scheme under Part 3 of the Housing Act 2004. If approved, the scheme would require most privately rented homes in the proposed designation areas to be licensed by the Council, unless exempt by law.' Consultation dates 'from Monday 3rd August at 12pm to Sunday 18th October 2026 at 11.59pm'. The page confirms the statutory position that 'Before introducing a Selective Licensing scheme, the law requires the Council to carry out public consultation', and that the consultation covers 'The proposed licence fee and payment arrangements', so no fee is yet set. Recorded with status 'proposed' rather than omitted, because landlords in the named wards need to know a decision is imminent. TRAP: the council page notes 'In areas of the borough where the article 4 direction applies planning permission must be obtained to convert a dwelling house to a smaller HMO'. Planning control, excluded. RE-CHECK SCHEDULED: after 18 October 2026.

notes: Harborough operates mandatory HMO licensing only. There is no selective licensing and no additional HMO licensing scheme. A licence is needed only where a property has five or more people forming more than one household.
research: The council states the trigger as the national mandatory test only: 'Some HMOs (not Section 257s) require a licence. A property needs a licence if it has 5 or more people who form more than 1 household (ie not all from 1 family)', with the standard exemption 'A purpose-built flat situated in a block comprising three or more self-contained flats is not subject to mandatory licensing even if that flat is an HMO.' No reference to selective or additional licensing. CORROBORATION from the council's own list of every licence it issues: the only housing entry is 'Apply for a house in multiple occupation licence'. There is no selective or additional licence application, which a designated scheme would require. NOTE ON LIMITS: the council's site search and its fees and charges page were intermittently unavailable ('Harborough DC is temporarily offline for scheduled routine maintenance') during checking, so a per-line fee schedule could not be read. This does not affect the conclusion, which rests on the licence trigger wording and the complete list of licences issued, but the fee page is worth a re-check.

notes: Harlow operates mandatory HMO licensing only, at £850. There is no selective or additional licensing scheme in force. The council's 2026 to 2027 corporate plan says it intends to introduce selective licensing, but nothing has been designated yet.
research: Checked with extra care. The live council page describes only the national mandatory test: 'Your property will need a mandatory licence if: it is rented to 5 people or more who form more than 1 household; some or all tenants share toilet, bathroom or kitchen facilities.' Its fee schedule has a single line: 'Mandatory licence for 5 or more occupants: £850 (reduced £600)', plus £80 per bedroom above six. No selective or additional fee. The register is 'the mandatory licence HMO public register', and the public register page offers only that plus temporary exemption notices. DIRECT POLICY STATEMENT: the Private Sector Housing Enforcement Policy, under the heading 'Selective licensing', states 'The Housing Act 2004 allows for the introduction of selective licensing schemes and additional licensing schemes. These are not currently considered appropriate to be adopted within Harlow, but this matter will be kept under review.' The document records 'This policy was last updated on 14 July 2023. The next review date is 13 March 2029', so it is current. FUTURE INTENTION, NOT A DESIGNATION: the corporate policy 'Building Harlow's Future', the main corporate framework for 2026 to 2027, includes the commitment 'Introduce a selective licensing scheme for private rented homes across Harlow.' That is an aspiration with no consultation, no designation notice, no confirmed area, no start date and no fee, so it is not recorded as a scheme, but landlords should watch for a statutory consultation. FALSE POSITIVE TRAP: the HMO page states applicants 'must have full planning permission to convert your property to a HMO - this applies to all applications because of a town-wide HMO Article 4 direction'. A town-wide Article 4 direction is planning control, not licensing.

notes: Hart operates mandatory HMO licensing only, starting at £893 for a licence covering five people. There is no selective licensing and no additional HMO licensing scheme, so smaller shared homes and ordinary private lets do not need a council licence.
research: The council states 'You may have to apply to us for a licence if you rent out a property as a house in multiple occupation to five or more people', the national mandatory threshold and the only trigger given. The published fee table is decisive because its lowest band is the mandatory threshold: 'Licence for 5 persons £893; Licence 6-10 persons £1,121; Licence 11-15 persons £1,344; Licence 16-20 persons £1,565; Licence 21+ persons £1,786', with renewals from £686. There is no fee band for three or four occupiers, which an additional licensing designation would require, and no selective licensing fee for ordinary private lets. Neither 'selective licensing' nor 'additional licensing' appears anywhere in the private sector housing section, and a sweep of 833 sitemap URLs returned no such page. TRAP CHECK: the 'How we work with landlords' page describes a rent deposit and letting incentive scheme where the council 'act as a free letting agent' for its clients. That is a voluntary landlord incentive service, not a licensing designation.
